global.headline: UAE HALTS ALL TRADE WITH IRAN OVER MISSILE FIRE AS PENTAGON CASUALTY COUNT JUMPS TO 757 WOUNDED
summary: The UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Wednesday it is halting all trade, commercial exchange and financial transactions with Iran "until further notice," in direct response to Tuesday's alleged Iranian ballistic-missile fire toward UAE territory — the first such barrage in months, which triggered nationwide shelter warnings before both missiles fell harmlessly into the sea. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei rejected the accusation as contrary to "the principle of good neighbourliness," and Tehran has not formally responded to the trade cut-off. The embargo is a major escalation: the UAE is one of Iran's largest trading partners, supplying more than 30% of Iran's imports, a blow to an economy already facing near-70% inflation and a 5.4% contraction.

Trump, asked about the war Wednesday, called the situation "so good" right now, confirmed the US is not in talks with Iran and has no plans to restart them, and ruled out extending the MOU's now-lapsed 60-day ceasefire window — while repeating his claim that the US holds "complete control" of the Strait of Hormuz, a claim Iran continues to dispute. The Pentagon's own numbers point the other way: its war-casualty database was updated Wednesday to show 18 US service members killed and more than 750 wounded since the war began on 28 February — the wounded count jumping over 130 in a single update, weeks after similar figures briefly vanished from the same database and were restored under bipartisan pressure.

A CNN analysis published Wednesday reports that Iran's hardline leadership, now running the war effort under new IRGC chief Ahmad Vahidi and new Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaie, is shifting explicitly toward an "offensive posture" — developing the capability to strike "on enemy soil," according to an adviser to Vahidi, and mobilising allied Houthi and Iraqi-militia pressure on Saudi targets. Brent crude extended a fourth straight day of gains to roughly US$91/barrel (S$123), with Hormuz-transit risk still the dominant driver.
global.geopolitical: Cutting off Iran's largest single trading partner turns a missile dispute into an economic one overnight, and lands as Iran's own hardliners talk openly of taking the war onto American soil — with Trump, for his part, professing the situation is "so good" while the Pentagon's own casualty count quietly climbs past 750.
global.socioeconomic: The UAE embargo strips an already-battered Iranian economy of the trading partner supplying nearly a third of its imports, compounding near-70% inflation and a shrinking GDP, while sustained Hormuz risk keeps Brent grinding toward US$92/barrel for economies far outside the Gulf.

global.headline: ISRAEL OPENS FIRST CRIMINAL PROBES INTO GAZA KILLINGS OF HIND RAJAB, 15 MEDICS — SAME DAY IT CLEARS SOLDIERS OVER AUSTRALIAN AID WORKER'S DEATH
summary: Israel's military said Wednesday it is opening its first-ever criminal investigations into troop conduct in the Gaza war, covering the February 2024 killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab and six of her relatives — trapped in a car and pleading for help by phone before being killed — and the May 2025 killing of 15 Palestinian paramedics whose bodies were later found in a mass grave. The military said it would not open criminal probes into three other incidents, including strikes that killed World Central Kitchen and Doctors Without Borders aid workers. Rajab's grandmother told the AP the domestic investigation "is not enough" and renewed calls for an international probe; independent UN Human Rights Council experts have said the killing may constitute a war crime.

The same day, Israel's military cleared its soldiers of criminal wrongdoing in the April 2024 strike that killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom and six World Central Kitchen colleagues — despite the IDF's own prior admissions of "serious failures to follow procedure, mistaken identification and errors in decision-making." Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia is "outraged," calling the decision "especially insulting" for landing on World Humanitarian Day, and said she would summon Israel's ambassador in Canberra while directing Australia's own ambassador in Israel to convey Canberra's objections directly.
global.geopolitical: Opening genuine criminal probes into two of the war's most internationally scrutinised killings, on the same day it closes the book on a third with no charges, hands Israel a mixed accountability record that satisfies neither victims' families nor allies like Australia, and keeps the question of an international investigation alive.
global.socioeconomic: For Gaza's aid operations, the pattern set by both rulings — narrow criminal accountability for the most publicised killings, none at all for aid-worker deaths — does little to ease the risk calculus humanitarian agencies already apply to operating in the strip, even as reconstruction and aid-delivery planning depend on exactly that access.

global.headline: ZELENSKY FIRES AIDE OVER CORRUPTION PROBE AS OUSTED DEFENCE CHIEF FEDOROV DEMANDS WARTIME ELECTIONS, SHARPEST CHALLENGE SINCE 2022
summary: President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed presidential-office deputy Iryna Mudra by decree Wednesday after anti-corruption investigators NABU and SAPO searched premises linked to her and a member of parliament, as part of a probe — codenamed "Forest Gump" — into an alleged "criminal organisation" involving senior officials in Zelensky's own office. Mudra, who oversaw legal affairs and judicial reform, is the latest senior aide swept up in a corruption investigation reaching the presidential administration.

The same day, Mykhailo Fedorov — the ousted former defence minister who built Ukraine's drone-warfare programme — published a video calling for wartime elections despite them being barred under martial law, warning of a "systemic crisis of governance" and saying "the old system... protects itself, it is scared of change." It is the most direct challenge to Zelensky's rule by a major political figure since Russia's 2022 invasion; one recent poll found Fedorov could beat Zelensky head-to-head in a runoff.
global.geopolitical: A sitting president firing his own aide over a corruption probe reaching his office, on the same day his own former defence minister publicly demands elections the law doesn't allow, exposes a governance crisis inside wartime Kyiv just as Ukraine depends on Western political and financial confidence to keep fighting.
global.socioeconomic: Corruption allegations reaching the presidential office risk complicating Ukraine's access to Western reconstruction and military financing, which is conditioned in part on anti-graft governance benchmarks — a domestic political rupture that lands squarely on the institutions the country's war financing runs through.

global.headline: SAFARI HELICOPTER CRASH IN KENYA KILLS ALL 7 ABOARD, INCLUDING 4 AMERICANS AND A US TV EXECUTIVE
summary: A helicopter carrying tourists from luxury safari operator &Beyond crashed in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe in Kenya's Samburu County on Tuesday, killing all seven aboard: four Americans, two Ecuadorians — one an Ecuadorian intelligence official — and the Kenyan pilot. Telemundo television executive José Alberto Suárez, 55, was among the Americans killed. Kenya's Civil Aviation Authority said the Eurocopter EC130 B4 had departed from Loisaba en route to Ewasonyiro; the cause of the crash has not been determined.
global.geopolitical: A multinational death toll — American, Ecuadorian and Kenyan — on a single luxury tourist flight puts Kenya's high-end safari-aviation safety record under fresh international scrutiny.
global.socioeconomic: Kenya's tourism sector, a major foreign-currency earner, depends heavily on the safety reputation of exactly this kind of premium safari travel; a fatal, still-unexplained crash involving a well-known operator is a reputational risk the industry will want resolved quickly.

global.headline: GOLD MINE COLLAPSE KILLS AT LEAST 30 IN CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC
summary: An artisanal gold-mining site collapsed in the Abba area of Central African Republic's Nana-Mambéré prefecture on Tuesday, killing at least 30 miners, local officials said; rescuers pulled bodies from the site over several hours and continued searching for others believed trapped, though hopes of finding survivors were fading. The site was one of many small-scale, government-unregulated mining operations in the country, where miners typically work without adequate protective equipment.
global.geopolitical: A mass-casualty accident at an unregulated mine underscores the Central African Republic government's limited practical control over its own resource-rich but conflict-scarred territory.
global.socioeconomic: Artisanal mining remains a livelihood of last resort for thousands in one of the world's poorest countries, and each such collapse repeats a now-familiar pattern: minimal safety enforcement, high casualties, and no structural change to an economy with few safer alternatives.

singapore.headline: MAS UNVEILS TAX BREAKS, HEDGE-FUND PROGRAMME AND NEW WORK-PASS TRACK TO DEFEND SINGAPORE'S ASSET-MANAGEMENT HUB STATUS
summary: The Monetary Authority of Singapore on Wednesday announced three measures to shore up Singapore's competitiveness as an asset-management hub: a tax exemption for profit-related returns from fund-management services to qualifying funds; a new hedge-fund investment programme meant to anchor leading hedge-fund managers here; and a new Investment Management Track under the Overseas Networks & Expertise (ONE) Pass to draw senior global investment talent.

MAS said the measures build on already-strong momentum: Singapore's asset-management industry has grown by an average 7.5% a year over the past five years to almost S$7 trillion under management, and now accounts for roughly 15% of the financial sector's output and 13% of its employment, even as international competition for the same mobile capital and talent intensifies.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic financial-regulatory matter, though it responds directly to competitive pressure from rival hubs such as Hong Kong, Dubai and London for the same asset-management flows.
singapore.socioeconomic: Tax breaks and an easier path for senior global talent lower the cost of doing business here for large fund managers, but the benefits concentrate among high-value financial-sector roles rather than broader employment, consistent with how the industry's growth has run well ahead of Singapore's overall workforce expansion.

singapore.headline: MSF UNVEILS 17 PILOT PROJECTS TO HOUSE AND SUPPORT ROUGH SLEEPERS AND HOMELESS YOUTH
summary: Singapore's Ministry of Social and Family Development on Wednesday unveiled 17 new pilot projects — funded by its $450,000 Partnership to Tackle Homelessness (PATH) Fund — aimed at rough sleepers and youth with nowhere to turn. They include a drop-in centre offering meals, showers and counselling; a scheme matching single rough sleepers with compatible co-tenants to speed access to public rental housing; and micro-jobs and apprenticeships to help build financial stability.

A parallel strand targets homeless youth specifically, offering mentoring, family mediation and vocational guidance for young people turned away by their own families. The projects, run by community groups including Bless Community Services and Hope Initiative Alliance, were unveiled at an appreciation event for MSF's community partners.
singapore.geopolitical: N/A — a domestic social-welfare policy matter.
singapore.socioeconomic: A dedicated fund testing multiple, targeted interventions rather than one blanket programme reflects growing recognition that rough sleeping and youth homelessness have distinct root causes — financial, relational and structural — that a single support scheme can't address at once.

singapore.headline: KOREAN WEDDING STUDIO'S SINGAPORE OUTLET ABRUPTLY SHUTS, CASE FIELDS 66 COMPLAINTS OVER $271,000 IN LOSSES
summary: Korea Artiz Studio's Singapore outlet on Bras Basah Road appears to have ceased operations, leaving couples who had paid in full for wedding photography packages unable to reach the company or use their booked sessions. A notice posted outside the studio cited internal operational issues and said staff had not received outstanding salaries. The Consumers Association of Singapore said it received 66 complaints between 14 and 18 August involving more than $271,000 in prepayment losses.

The Singapore closure follows the sudden shutdown of the chain's Taiwan outlet on 10 August. Founded in Busan in 2008, Korea Artiz Studio expanded to Singapore in 2017. CASE said affected consumers can seek assistance through its hotline or website.
singapore.socioeconomic: The case extends a now-familiar pattern of sudden prepayment-dependent business failures — echoing this year's beauty-industry closures — leaving consumers with limited recourse and again raising questions about safeguards for large upfront wedding-services payments.

singapore.headline: JAPAN HOME SHUTTERS MULTIPLE SINGAPORE OUTLETS AMID REPORTS OF VALU$ TAKEOVER
summary: Household retail chain Japan Home has closed several outlets across Singapore since June, with five stores — at Hougang Mall, Century Square, Northpoint City, HarbourFront Centre and Buangkok Square — running closing-down sales announced on the company's Facebook page. A Business Times check of nine locations found six closed for stocktaking and three shuttered outright.

Staff at some locations told reporters the stores may reopen under joint management with rival Value Dollar (Valu$), with Valu$ stock and uniforms already visible at some sites. Japan Home operated 34 outlets islandwide before the closures began; neither company has confirmed the scope or timeline of any takeover.
singapore.socioeconomic: A homegrown value-retail chain closing stores even as a rival appears to be absorbing its locations points to consolidation pressure in Singapore's budget-retail segment, likely driven by the same rent and cost pressures that have squeezed other physical retailers this year.

word.definition: To forbid or prohibit something officially, especially by law or decree; to condemn or denounce as dangerous.
word.etymology: From Latin proscribere, "to publish in writing, outlaw," from pro- ("before, in public") + scribere ("to write") — originally the Roman practice of publicly posting the names of those condemned to death or exile.
word.example: The UAE didn't just protest Tuesday's alleged Iranian missile fire — it proscribed all trade and financial dealings with Tehran outright, turning a diplomatic complaint into an overnight economic embargo against a partner that supplies nearly a third of Iran's imports.
